Penn State flood research in Harrisburg

Helping Harrisburg see where a flood will reach

When the National Weather Service forecasts a high crest on the Susquehanna, city staff have a day or two to work out which streets will flood and who lives there. We are a Penn State team building a tool that does that work from public flood maps and building records. This page shows an early mockup. It is a design for discussion, and the City of Harrisburg has not endorsed it.

Try the mockup

Background

Why Harrisburg?

Harrisburg sits on the east bank of the Susquehanna, and the river has flooded the city many times. In June 1972 the remnants of Hurricane Agnes pushed the river to 33.27 feet at the Harrisburg gage, the highest crest on record. In September 2011 the remnants of Tropical Storm Lee brought it to 25.17 feet, and the riverfront flooded again.

The city also floods from heavy rain. Much of Harrisburg has combined sewers, where sewage and stormwater share one pipe. In a big storm those pipes fill, and the mix spills into Paxton Creek and the river. Capital Region Water's model estimates that about 602 million gallons overflowed this way in 2025.

This project builds on work Penn State has been doing with Harrisburg community groups since May 2025, when Chingwen Cheng's Co-Design Harrisburg workshop brought together about 20 city and state staff, nonprofit and community leaders to talk about community resilience. Better flood warning and the combined sewer overflows were among the problems they raised.

What's New

What does this add to the flood maps that already exist?

Harrisburg already has good forecasts. The National Weather Service forecasts the river crest, federal agencies have mapped how far the water spreads at each level, and AI forecasts such as Google's Flood Hub and private weather services keep improving. We use all of these as they are and don't make a new forecast.

The hard part comes after the forecast. Someone at the city has to pull together the flood map, building records, census data and past storms, work out who is in the way, and tell crews and residents what to do, all under time pressure. That step is still done by hand, and it is the step we are building for. The table below lists the tools that already exist, what each one gives the city, and what is still left for staff to do on the day of a flood.

Existing toolWhat it gives the cityWhat is still left for staff
NWS river forecast and the NWS/USGS flood mapsThe expected crest at the Harrisburg gage, and the area the river covers at each stage.Working out which buildings sit in that area, who lives there, who will need help leaving, and what to tell crews and residents.
AI forecasts (Google Flood Hub, private weather services)Earlier and often better river forecasts.The same work as the row above. A better forecast still has to be turned into a plan for specific blocks.
GIS overlays and dashboards (including FEMA's Hazus)Maps and counts for questions someone set up ahead of time.Any new question on flood day needs a person with GIS skills to build the query, read the result and write it up.
Capital Region Water's sewer model and annual overflow reportsWhere and how much the combined sewers overflowed in past storms.Judging which streets and basements are likely to flood in tonight's storm, which the river maps can't show.
Published methods that estimate first-floor height from street photosA way to replace the default heights in the national building inventory.Adapting and checking them for Harrisburg's pre-1940 rowhouses with basements, and connecting the results to flood-day decisions.

Isn't this a GIS problem?

Part of it is. Finding which buildings sit inside a mapped flood is a spatial join, and we do that with ordinary GIS code so the counts are exact and repeatable. What GIS doesn't do is the rest of the work on flood day. Staff ask questions nobody built a layer for in advance, such as how many people over 65 live on the blocks the river reaches at 23 feet, or which sewer outfalls near those blocks overflowed most in 2025. The assistant writes and runs the GIS query for each question, reads the result, and explains it with a source for every statement, so a staff member without GIS training gets an answer in minutes. It says plainly when the data don't cover something. It then turns the same results into a short briefing for crews and draft alerts for residents in English and Spanish, and after a flood it helps inspectors turn photos and notes into FEMA damage forms, with the inspector confirming every value. The flood extents and counts always come from the agencies' maps, so the assistant explains the numbers and does not make them up.

The public data also have gaps the assistant can help fill. Every one of the 111 homes the river reaches at 23 feet is listed in the national building inventory with the same default first-floor height of 2 feet, because the inventory has no measured value for them. Whether water comes in the front door depends on that height. Researchers, including at Penn State, have published ways to estimate first-floor height from street-level photos. We plan to adapt them to Harrisburg's rowhouses and check the estimates against measurements on the ground.

How will we know it helps?

We will run the same flood scenario as a tabletop exercise with city staff twice, once with the current manual process and once with the assistant. We will time how long each takes to reach an action plan (our target is under 30 minutes, against the hours it takes now) and check which vulnerable households each plan reaches. We will also replay the 2004 and 2011 river floods and recent storms in Capital Region Water's records, compare the blocks the briefings flag with where flooding happened, and check every statement in every briefing against its source.

Here is what you can try in the mockup.

A briefing for city staff

A short summary with its sources, written for Public Works and emergency management. Staff can ask it follow-up questions in the Ask tab. There is also a draft alert for residents in English and Spanish. Staff edit and approve everything before it goes out.

Which buildings the river reaches

Choose a forecast crest, from minor flooding up to the 1972 Agnes level. The map marks each building the mapped flood reaches, and the counts underneath show how many are homes and roughly how many people sleep there.

Where the sewers overflow

Choose a rain forecast and see the 2025 storm that came closest to it. Each sewer outfall is sized by how much Capital Region Water's model says spilled there.

After the water goes down

A list of where to inspect first, and help filling out FEMA damage forms from photos and notes. The inspector checks every value.

Data

Where do the numbers come from?

Everything on the maps comes from public data that federal agencies and Capital Region Water already publish.

  • The river flood maps were made by the National Weather Service with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Baltimore District), USGS, the Susquehanna River Basin Commission and PA Silver Jackets. They show flooding from the main river only, so Paxton Creek and other streams are left out.
  • Building locations, types and the number of people who live in them come from the Army Corps' National Structure Inventory. Which neighborhoods may need more help comes from the CDC's Social Vulnerability Index (2022, ranked within Pennsylvania).
  • A building counts as "reached" when the mapped flood touches it. That tells you where water gets to, which is different from how badly a building is damaged.
  • For the 25 ft and 33.3 ft crests we read the Weather Service's flood depth maps ourselves. We count a building if water touches it or comes within 10 meters, which gives a range. At the crests where the Weather Service publishes its own counts, our range takes in theirs (43 to 59 against 51 at 20 ft, and 145 to 217 against 202 at 23 ft).
  • The sewer overflow numbers come from Capital Region Water's 2025 Annual CSO Status Report and its City Beautiful H2O Program Plan. Capital Region Water has not yet reviewed how we use them here.
  • We drafted the sample briefings, alerts and answers with an AI model (Claude), working from these data. The inspection screen uses made-up values to show how it would work.
  • Still to build are the AI agent that would write the briefings, the inspection helper, and maps of which streets and basements flood in heavy rain.
